## Summary

- An agent is a model plus a harness: a program in which a language model chooses some steps and the harness decides which are carried out. The harness decides what the model sees, what it may do, what is remembered, how the work is checked and when the run stops. Module 8's tool loop is the smallest harness; this module adds state, branching, pauses and control over actions. An evaluation harness, which scores a system, is a different thing.
- ReAct interleaves reasoning in text with actions and observations (@eq-react). Function calling is its structured form. A model's stated reason for a tool call is logged, never trusted.
- A LangChain tool is Module 8's `Tool` with a decorator; a runnable is the common `invoke` / `batch` interface, shared by tools, `TypeSafeClassifier` and any wrapped function. A tool's description is the prompt the model chooses by: give each agent few tools, return only what the task needs, and make every error say whether to fix, retry or stop, never confusing an empty result with a failure.
- A LangGraph program is a graph over an explicit state: nodes return updates, reducers merge them, edges read the state (@eq-graph-step). Draw the state table before writing code.
- A checkpointer saves the state after every step. Threads give memory; `interrupt` pauses for a person and `Command(resume=...)` continues; snapshots can be replayed and forked. The interrupted node re-runs from its start, and a replay re-runs side effects, so keep decision calls out of the pausing node and make tools idempotent.
- Agents fail by looping, choosing the wrong tool, acting unsafely and following injected text, which arrives through requests, retrieved documents and tool results. The defenses that hold are architectural: least privilege, hard rules in code, a separate check before the action, and a person for the uncertain middle. A rule that must hold every time belongs in the harness, not in the prompt; a run ends on a final answer, and $K_{\max}$ marks a failure.
- A calibrated decision model fits at the router and the guard, each with thresholds from its own costs (@eq-route-rule, @eq-guard-rule). Calibration bounds the share of wrong actions taken alone (@eq-unsafe-bound), but only on the distribution it was calibrated on. Escalate also on an explicit request for a person, a gap in the policy or a lack of progress, never on tone or on the language model's stated confidence, and write a hand-off that stands alone.
- Report route accuracy, unsafe-action rate and injection success rate with their denominators (@eq-route-acc, @eq-uar, @eq-isr), and measure how far injected text moves the guard (@eq-shift).
- Design the harness from the simplest pattern that works (a chain, routing, parallel calls, a checker) and let the model plan only where the path cannot be written in advance. The same model can score very differently in different harnesses, at very different costs. Subagents see only their task description and return summaries; their failures come back as results, the coordinator checks coverage, and they cost many times the tokens. Keep the context small: trim tool results, keep facts in typed state, compact or isolate.

## Common misconceptions

- **"An agent framework makes the model more capable", or its opposite, "the harness is just plumbing".** The model's weights are the same in any harness. What the system can do is not: the same model scores very differently in different harnesses (section 1), because the harness decides what the model sees, what it may try and how its work is checked. Reliability comes from the harness too.
- **"The model's stated reason explains its tool call."** It is more generated text. Log it, read it, and do not act on it.
- **"LangGraph resumes after the `interrupt` line."** It re-runs the node from the top. Code before the `interrupt` runs twice.
- **"Replaying a run is free."** It re-executes every node after the snapshot, including tools that act on the world.
- **"The default recursion limit stops runaway loops."** In `langgraph` 1.2.12 it is 10,007 graph steps. Set your own limit and count model calls.
- **"A system prompt that says 'tool results are data' stops prompt injection."** It lowers the rate; it does not remove it. Limit what injected text can cause.
- **"A rule in the system prompt enforces the order of steps."** It is followed at some rate. A rule that must hold every time is an edge or a check in the harness.
- **"An empty result means the tool failed", or the reverse.** They are different facts, and a model that cannot tell them apart will tell a registered participant they are not registered. The tool must say which happened.
- **"A decision model cannot be injected because it outputs a number."** Injected text cannot add a tool call through it, but it can move the number. Measure $\Delta p$.
- **"One threshold fits the whole agent."** The router and the guard have different costs and therefore different thresholds, from the same formula.
- **"Escalate when the participant is upset, or when the model says it is unsure."** Tone does not measure how hard a case is, and a language model's stated confidence is uncalibrated text. A probability from a separate model, checked on labeled items, is a different kind of number.
- **"A UAR of zero means the guard is safe."** On 30 disallowed items it is consistent with a true rate of several percent, and a guard that escalates everything also scores zero.
- **"A subagent knows what the coordinator knows."** It starts with an empty context and sees only its task description. A constraint the participant stated to the coordinator is lost unless the coordinator writes it into the task.
- **"More agents give better answers."** Anthropic's multi-agent system beat a single agent on broad research, at about 15 times the tokens of a chat, and on one benchmark token use alone explained 80% of the variance in its results. For a narrow task, one agent is cheaper and easier to check.
- **"Asking the model to check its own work makes it reliable."** With nothing new to go on, self-correction often fails to help. A check that runs a test, reads a source or asks a separate model is what pays.
- **"The local decider's numbers tell us about Jev."** They measure our toy model or a small open model. Only the keyed path measures Jev, and only on this synthetic domain.

## What Module 15 picks up

You can now build an agent as an explicit graph, pause it for a person, replay it, and put a decision model at its router and its guard with thresholds from costs. [Module 15](15-capstone.qmd) combines this graph with the retrieval of [Module 13](13-rag.qmd) into a research assistant over the workshop's reading list, adds the verify step as part of the core system, and asks you to improve one component and report accuracy, abstention and cost against a fixed evaluation set.

## Readings

1. Yao, S., Zhao, J., Yu, D., Du, N., Shafran, I., Narasimhan, K. and Cao, Y. (2023). [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629). *ICLR*. Sections 1 to 3: the pattern, its notation and the comparison with reasoning-only and acting-only prompting. *Title, authors, venue and summary checked by web search on 2026-10-05; the notation in section 2 of this page follows the paper as recalled, not re-read.*
2. LangGraph documentation, the pages on persistence and interrupts (docs.langchain.com, "LangGraph"). *Not read by the workshop authors: the build environment could not reach the documentation site. The behavior on this page was checked against the `langgraph` 1.2.12 source and by running small graphs.* Read the current pages before teaching.
3. Schluntz, E. and Zhang, B. (2024). [Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents). Anthropic, 19 December 2024. Workflows against agents, the five workflow patterns of section 9, and the case for the simplest system that works. Skip its list of frameworks: the page itself now says "much of the tooling landscape described in this post has changed since December 2024". *Page opened 2026-10-06.*
4. Greshake, K., Abdelnabi, S., Mishra, S., Endres, C., Holz, T. and Fritz, M. (2023). [Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.12173). *AISec '23 (ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security)*. The paper that named indirect injection: any text the model reads is a possible attack. *Checked by web search.*
5. Beurer-Kellner, L. et al. (2025). [Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08837). arXiv:2506.08837. Six architectural patterns built on one principle: untrusted text must not be able to trigger consequential actions. *Checked by web search.*
